# Project Kestrel — Buyer's Review of Seller's SPA Update and Disclosure Letter

**Privileged & confidential — prepared for Wattlebridge Holdings deal team**

Before the substance, a framing point. The Seller's preamble asserts these terms are "FINAL," "settled at principal level," and "not intended to be re-opened," and recites a "market context" paragraph. Treat this as negotiating anchor, not fact. Several of the "standard market" claims are simply wrong for a deal of this type (I flag them below), and nothing stops us marking up a draft. Please confirm with your principals whether any of these were in fact conceded at principal level — my working assumption is that they were not, and the Disclosure Letter itself contradicts several of the Seller's "it's handled" assertions.

The two most damaging structural issues are the **combination of (a) general disclosure of the entire data room and (b) a deemed/constructive buyer-knowledge bar**. Together these largely gut the warranty package. I deal with those first.

---

## A. Structural issues that hollow out the warranties

### 1. Deemed buyer knowledge — Clause 8.3 (push back hard)
The Seller wants no claim for any matter the Buyer "or its advisers had knowledge" of, "including any matter **discoverable** from the data room or public records." This is *constructive* knowledge, not actual knowledge. It means anything we could theoretically have found defeats a claim. The Seller's claim that this is "standard" is incorrect — a deemed-discoverability bar is aggressive and not market.

**Position:** Limit to the *actual* knowledge of a short list of named deal-team individuals, as at signing. Delete "discoverable," "advisers," and "public records." A warranty we can't rely on because we "should have found" the problem is worthless.

### 2. General/sweeping disclosure — Disclosure Letter 1.1, 1.2 (push back hard)
Clause 1.1 purports to disclose "**every fact, matter and circumstance** contained or referred to" in the entire data room (DD-002 to DD-012), plus the Accounts and public registers. Clause 1.4 then says nothing in the letter admits anything. So the Seller discloses the whole room against all warranties but admits nothing — the mirror image of issue 1. Anything buried in the data room becomes "disclosed," so no claim.

**Position:** Reject general/data-room-wide disclosure. Require **specific disclosure only**, disclosed against identified warranties, and a "**fairly disclosed**" standard (disclosed with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope of the matter and allow a reasonable buyer to assess it). Public registers should not be a disclosure source.

### 3. Exclusive remedy / non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature" — 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (push back)
Applying non-reliance, exclusive-remedy and the limitations to *all* claims will, on its face, capture fraud and fraudulent misrepresentation.

**Position:** A universal **fraud carve-out** from every limitation, cap, time bar, disclosure and knowledge qualification (fraud, fraudulent misrepresentation, wilful concealment/default). This is non-negotiable and genuinely standard.

---

## B. Caps, baskets and time limits

### 4. Fundamental / title warranties capped and time-limited as general — "administrative simplicity" (push back hard)
This is the most objectionable "market" claim. Capacity and **title** warranties should be **uncapped (or capped at 100% of price)** and survive for a long/indefinite period. If title to the shares fails, we could lose the entire company yet recover only AUD 4.8m. "Administrative simplicity" is not a reason to accept catastrophic downside.

**Position:** Fundamental/title warranties — cap = 100% of price (AUD 24m); limitation period 7 years (or indefinite for title).

### 5. General cap — Clause 12.1 (negotiate)
20% / AUD 4.8m sits within a defensible range but at the Seller-friendly end only after we also fix issues 1–4; otherwise the cap is academic. Push toward a higher cap and, more importantly, ring-fence the specific-indemnity items below so they sit **outside** the general cap.

### 6. Basket / de minimis — Clause 12.2 (negotiate)
De minimis AUD 25k and basket AUD 250k (~1% of price) are roughly market. But the Seller proposes an **excess-only** basket (deductible — recover only above AUD 250k).

**Position:** Seek a **tipping/first-dollar basket** (once AUD 250k is reached, recover from dollar one). At minimum, trade this against the cap.

### 7. Time limits — Clause 12.3 / 13 (push back)
18 months for general warranties is acceptable. But "any limitation applying to Claims applies to **all** Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" sweeps **tax** and **fundamental** warranties into 18 months. That is not market.

**Position:** Tax warranties and the tax covenant/indemnity survive to the **statutory limitation period** (c. 7 years); fundamental/title as per issue 4. General and business warranties 18 months is fine.

---

## C. Debt, leakage and funds flow (debt-free/cash-free baseline)

### 8. Riverlark facility ~AUD 3.2m — Clause 2 / 7 (push back hard)
The Disclosure Letter confirms the facility is **not repaid and security not discharged**, yet the Seller proposes a release "following Completion." Under a debt-free/cash-free deal we will not take the company with undischarged security on a promise.

**Position:** Repayment in full **at Completion** out of the proceeds via the funds flow, with an **executed discharge/release of security delivered at Completion** (and payout letter pre-Completion). The AUD 3.2m reduces the equity proceeds — confirm it is reflected in the funds flow.

### 9. DD-005 Completion bonuses AUD 420k — Funds flow (push back)
The Seller says these are "a matter for the Seller" and deliberately omits them from the funds flow. But they are **triggered by Completion** — classic change-of-control/transaction leakage that the *company* will likely bear post-Completion. The disclosure also leaves **payroll tax, superannuation and on-costs** open.

**Position:** Treat the bonuses **plus all on-costs (super, payroll tax)** as a Seller liability — either paid by Seller pre-Completion or deducted in the funds flow as a debt-like/leakage item. Get a specific indemnity for any shortfall and gross-up for on-costs.

### 10. Sandbar supplier renewals AUD 330k — DD-008 / DD-011 (investigate)
Three "related" renewals of exactly AUD 110k each. The disclosure flags they should be "read together" and does **not** confirm they are ordinary-course, terminable or unavoidable. The identical sizing invites the question of whether they were split to sit under an individual consent/materiality threshold.

**Position:** Obtain the contracts; confirm term, termination rights, accrual and whether committed around Completion. If new committed spend, treat as leakage or require it as a pre-Completion conduct/consent item.

---

## D. Business-critical specific risks (need specific indemnities / conditions)

### 11. Bluefen change-of-control — Clause 3 / 6.3 (push back hard)
Bluefen is **~AUD 3.6m / ~30% of FY26 revenue** and has a change-control consent requirement (cl 11.2, conditions 11.3). The Disclosure Letter confirms there is **no final written consent and the conditions are not satisfied**. Yet the Seller offers only "reasonable endeavours" and deems consent "satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent" — ignoring the 11.3 conditions.

**Position:** Make obtaining the Bluefen consent (consent **and** satisfaction of the 11.3 conditions) a **Condition Precedent to Completion**, upgrade to "best endeavours," and if it can't be a CP, price-protect it (retention/earn-out adjustment and/or specific uncapped indemnity for loss of Bluefen). Losing 30% of revenue post-Completion would materially re-set the valuation.

### 12. Ironquay IP — Clause 11.1 / DL 4 (push back)
Under DD-004 cl 7.3, SOW3 **Project Materials (IP) only transfer on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee**; DD-010 shows AUD 180k open, with no proof of payment or confirmatory assignment. The real risk isn't the AUD 180k fee — it's that **the company may not own SOW3 IP** at all. The Seller's indemnity, limited to the SOW3 payment, does not cover loss of the IP. For a SaaS target, IP ownership is the core asset.

**Position:** Pre-Completion, obtain proof of payment **and** a confirmatory IP assignment; a specific IP-ownership warranty; and a specific indemnity covering loss/impairment of the SOW3 IP (not just the fee), outside the general cap.

### 13. Export/privacy incident DD-006 — Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (push back hard)
A download link to ~1,240 personal records (names, business emails, roles, activity) sent to an unintended external address. The Seller characterises it as "preliminary" and "not expected to be material." Under the Privacy Act / Notifiable Data Breaches scheme this can trigger **assessment and OAIC/individual notification obligations** and regulatory/remediation exposure; the disclosure itself concedes scope, access and notification are unresolved.

**Position:** Do **not** accept the "not material" characterisation. Require (i) completion of the investigation and a status report pre-Completion, (ii) a data-protection compliance warranty, and (iii) a **specific indemnity for the incident** (regulatory fines, notification/remediation, third-party claims) sitting **outside** the basket and cap.

### 14. Title evidence — DD-012 (verify)
Title is evidenced only by the share register, and the Seller notes we have not done our own verification.

**Position:** Current ASIC/PPSR searches; confirm no encumbrances over the shares; a strong, uncapped title warranty (per issue 4).

### 15. Lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009) — (verify, lower priority)
A share sale usually doesn't trigger assignment/consent, but both contracts should be checked for **change-of-control** notice/consent/termination triggers (the lease has a notification obligation; Mossvale restricts assignment). Low risk but confirm, and comply with any notice obligation.

---

## E. Summary of recommendations (priority order)

**Reject outright / non-negotiable:**
1. Fraud carve-out from all limitations, disclosure and knowledge qualifications.
2. Delete constructive/deemed buyer knowledge (8.3) — actual knowledge of named individuals only; delete "discoverable"/public records/advisers.
3. Reject whole-data-room general disclosure — specific disclosure only, "fairly disclosed" standard.
4. Fundamental/title warranties uncapped (or 100% of price) with long/indefinite survival; tax to statutory period.

**Deal-protection must-haves:**
5. Bluefen consent + 11.3 conditions as a Condition Precedent (best endeavours); fallback specific indemnity/price protection — ~30% of revenue at stake.
6. Riverlark AUD 3.2m repaid and security discharged **at** Completion, reflected in funds flow.
7. Specific indemnities outside the cap/basket for: the privacy incident (DD-006), Ironquay SOW3 IP ownership (not just the fee), and the DD-005 bonuses plus on-costs.
8. DD-005 bonuses + super/payroll tax treated as Seller liability/leakage in the funds flow.

**Negotiate / trade:**
9. General cap — push above 20% and keep specific indemnities outside it.
10. Tipping basket rather than excess-only; de minimis/basket otherwise acceptable.
11. Separate tax covenant and IP warranty suite (core SaaS asset).

**Verify in diligence:**
12. Sandbar renewals (ordinary-course / terminable / split-to-avoid-threshold question), lease and Mossvale change-of-control triggers, title/PPSR searches.

**Correct the record with the Seller:** the preamble's "market" claims on fundamental-warranty caps, tax survival and buyer knowledge are not standard; I'd reply that we do not accept the "FINAL / not to be re-opened" framing and are marking up accordingly.

If helpful, I can turn this into a markup/issues list against the clause numbers or draft the specific-indemnity and CP language for items 5–8. Want me to prepare that next?

# Project Kestrel – Seller Review: Departures from Buyer Playbook

Below are the departures identified, with reasoning, followed by a summary of recommended actions.

---

## 1. General Warranty Cap: 20% / AUD 4,800,000 (Clause 12.1)

**Departure:** The Seller drops the cap from our starting position of 25% / AUD 6,000,000 to 20% / AUD 4,800,000 — unconditionally, without prior written authority from our principal Amelia Frost, and without identifying the draft that would trigger the fallback.

**Reasoning:** Our playbook reserves the 20% cap as a conditional concession only with documented authorisation. Unconditional surrender of the starting position undermines our baseline protection. Any claim under the lower cap is narrower than the default market expectation for an AUD 24M acquisition.

---

## 2. Thresholds: de minimis AUD 25,000; basket AUD 250,000 (Clause 12.2)

**Departure:** Both thresholds are materially higher than ours — de minimis AUD 25,000 (ours AUD 5,000) and basket AUD 250,000 (ours AUD 50,000), with seller liable only from the excess once exceeded.

**Reasoning:** With such high thresholds, most genuine claims — even modest ones like the export incident below — would fall below the de minimis. Combined with the low cap and short limitation period (see §3), the practical effect is to insulate the Seller from a broad range of claims beyond what our baseline contemplates. Even where baskets apply, our standard is seller-liable-from-first-dollar; theirs is net-excess-only.

---

## 3. Time Limits: 18 months general; collapsed into general for Title (Clause 12.3 / 13)

**Departure A (General):** The Seller adopts 18 months unconditional rather than 24 months standard, with 18 months available only as a fallback requiring Amelia Frost written approval. By achieving the fallback unconditionally, they have secured a materially shorter limitation period than our default.

**Departure B (Fundamental/Title):** The Seller proposes capacity and title warranties be subject to the *same* caps and time limits as general warranties — i.e., 20% cap, 18-month period, and into the same basket/de minimis scheme.

**Reasoning:** Our position requires fundamental/title claims to be in a *separate* regime: 100% cap, at least six years, outside the general basket/de minimis/knowledge bar. Collapsing title into general warranties with sub-caps and a shorter period produces materially weaker title protections and may be commercially unacceptable to the buyer given the transaction's scale.

---

## 4. Limitations & Reliance Clause (Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)

**Departure:** The Seller asserts limitations, exclusive remedies and non-reliance apply to *all Claims of any nature*.

**Reasoning:** While our playbook does not specify a clause number, our principle is that fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct must be carved out to the maximum extent enforceable and cannot be waived. The Seller's framing risks washing out that carve-out by collapsing all claims — including potentially fundamental/title — into a single limitations clause. We should push to confirm the carve-out survives and is not subject to a waiver, and that it extends to fundamental/title claims as well.

---

## 5. Disclosure: General / Whole-Data-Room Approach (Schedule 7)

**Departure:** The Seller's Disclosure Letter relies on *general* disclosure of the indexed electronic data room and public registers, with Schedule 7 providing that disclosing "every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room".

**Reasoning:** Our playbook explicitly rejects whole-data-room, public-register or prudent-search deemed disclosure in favour of *specific* fair disclosure. The Seller's approach also admits nothing in the letter (*"[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach..."*) and, critically, the letter's admission of facts is rendered meaningless if every data room document is treated as disclosed. We should insist on specific disclosures for each DD item, with admitted facts tied to the disclosure schedule, not blanket references.

---

## 6. Buyer Knowledge (Clause 8.3)

**Departure:** A blanket Buyer-knowledge exclusion — "the Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records".

**Reasoning:** Our playbook mandates deletion of blanket exclusions; any qualifier needs named Seller knowledge persons + reasonable enquiry, and must never excuse title, capacity, fraud or specific indemnities. A blanket exclusion effectively neutralises the DD process and may cover title defects the Buyer has discovered independently. This conflicts directly with our title position (§14 below). We should push to delete the blanket exclusion entirely and require named knowledge persons with reasonable enquiries for any qualification.

---

## 7. Bluefen Change-Control Consent (Clause 3 / 6.3; DD-002)

**Departure A (Spirit):** The Seller treats the consent as satisfied on delivery of counterparty written consent using "reasonable endeavours", and the Disclosure Letter states "As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied."

**Departure B (Consistency):** The clause and the disclosure letter contradict each other.

**Reasoning:** Our playbook requires *effective consent AND evidence that associated conditions are satisfied* **before Completion**. Reasonable endeavour alone is insufficient for a material customer consent. The Seller has not provided either requirement, let alone pre-Completion. We should push to require an effective Bluefen consent with evidence of satisfied conditions, in writing, prior to Completion, with enforcement if absent.

---

## 8. Riverlark Bank Facility (Clause 2 / 7; DD-003)

**Departure:** The Seller proposes a release to follow Completion with no requirement for:
- Current payout (the facility is ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding);
- Direct repayment from Completion funds;
- Effective security release;
- Irrevocable undertaking for any post-completion release.

**Reasoning:** A release after Completion, without fund repayment, without our approval framework, and without an irrevocable undertaking, provides weak security and delayed repayment. ## Overall assessment

**Do not accept this package as agreed or final.** The Seller’s claims about market practice and principal-level agreement are unverified counterparty assertions, not Buyer authority. Neither the **20% cap nor the 18-month claims period is authorised**: both require Amelia Frost’s prior written approval identifying the draft, and none has been given.

The Disclosure Letter also contradicts several reassuring statements in the Seller update. Disclosure of an unresolved issue does not cure it or satisfy a Completion condition. The underlying DD documents and current evidence should be refreshed before conclusions are drawn.

## Material departures and pushback

| Issue | Assessment and recommended Buyer position |
|---|---|
| **General warranty cap — cl 12.1** | AUD 4.8m/20% is an **unauthorised fallback**, not our opening position. Restore **AUD 6m/25%**. Do not treat the matching fallback figure as clearance of the wider package. |
| **Thresholds — cl 12.2** | AUD 25,000 de minimis and AUD 250,000 excess-only basket materially reduce recovery. Restore **AUD 5,000 de minimis and AUD 50,000 tipping basket**, with recovery from the first dollar once exceeded. |
| **General claims period — cls 12.3/13** | Restore **24 months after Completion**. Eighteen months requires Amelia’s written approval. Reject the proposed presumption that limitations apply to every category of Claim: it risks importing general restrictions into separately negotiated protections. |
| **Fundamental/title claims** | Reject administrative simplicity as a reason to dilute ownership and capacity protection. Require a **separate 100% cap and at least six years**, outside the general basket, de minimis and buyer-knowledge bar. |
| **Fraud and remedies — cls 9.3/12.8/20.5** | The “all Claims” wording lacks essential exceptions. Expressly carve out **fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct** from all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedies and non-reliance provisions, to the maximum extent enforceable. **This protection cannot be waived.** |
| **Disclosure — Schedule 7; letter §§1.1–1.2** | Reject blanket disclosure of the data room, accounts, registers and public records. Require **specific fair disclosure**, identifying the relevant warranty and enough detail to understand the nature and scope of the exception. Availability or discoverability alone must not defeat a claim. Ensure disclosure does not discharge Completion obligations or specific indemnities. |
| **Buyer knowledge — cl 8.3** | Delete the blanket exclusion for Buyer/adviser knowledge and discoverable matters. It shifts diligence risk to Buyer and compounds the deemed-disclosure provisions. Any negotiated knowledge qualification must follow the playbook’s named Seller knowledge-person and reasonable-enquiry requirements, and must never excuse title, capacity, fraud or a specific indemnity. |
| **Separate claim categories; Tax/IP** | Reject the assertion that Tax/IP are settled under the general regime. **Both remain open; unlimited liability is not assumed.** Keep Title, Tax, IP, payment obligations and covenants distinct, with express scope and priority provisions preventing a hidden general-regime override. |

## Transaction-specific protections

### 1. Bluefen: unresolved material Completion condition
Bluefen represents approximately **AUD 3.6m/30% of FY26 revenue**. The letter confirms that neither final written consent nor evidence of satisfaction of its conditions has been supplied.

**Push back:** require effective change-control consent **and evidence that all associated conditions are satisfied before Completion**. Delivery of a conditional consent is insufficient; reasonable endeavours do not substitute for the required outcome. Review the consent for adverse conditions rather than merely checking receipt.

### 2. Riverlark: repayment and release must be coordinated
Approximately **AUD 3.2m** remains outstanding; there is no final discharge. A promise of a later release leaves Buyer exposed to continuing security after paying the price.

**Push back:** obtain a current payout statement, provide for **direct repayment from Completion funds**, and require effective security releases. A post-Completion release requires both an **irrevocable undertaking and Amelia’s approval**; neither is established here.

### 3. Employee bonuses: funds-flow omission
The **AUD 420,000** conditional bonuses are absent from the draft funds flow. Calling them “a matter for the Seller” does not establish who actually funds the liability.

**Push back:** verify which Completion/continued-employment conditions trigger payment and determine applicable payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs. Include the bonuses **plus triggered on-costs as an explicit line item or demonstrably Seller-funded obligation**, aligned with the price mechanics to avoid omission or double counting.

### 4. Ironquay: payment uncertainty and IP ownership risk
Transfer of SOW3 materials is conditional on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. The AUD 180,000 “open” entry **does not independently establish payment or non-payment**. No receipt or confirmatory assignment is supplied.

**Push back:** obtain independent payment evidence and confirm the rights transferred. Preserve the SOW3 cure through verified payment and effective transfer/assignment documentation, while **broadening the indemnity beyond the specified payment to the associated ownership and rights exposure**. Do not treat the narrow indemnity as a substitute for securing the IP.

### 5. Export/privacy incident: investigate without prejudging
The preliminary record identifies an unintended recipient and potentially about **1,240 records**, but does not establish access, exact scope or notification obligations. The Seller’s “not expected to be material” statement is unsupported reassurance.

**Push back:** require log and evidence preservation, a documented investigation, appropriate containment and continuing updates through Completion. Assess access, data scope and applicable notification duties on the evidence. **Do not assume a confirmed breach, harm, notification duty or any numeric demand in either direction.**

### 6. Sandbar renewals: classification requires evidence
Three renewals total **AUD 330,000**. The letter does not substantiate the update’s ordinary-course characterisation.

**Push back:** read DD-008 and DD-011 together; establish timing, scope, accrual, termination rights and whether commitments are unavoidable. Then assess treatment under the agreed price mechanics. **No automatic Debt classification or price deduction.**

### 7. Title: internal register is insufficient verification
DD-012 records Harbourglass as the 100% shareholder, but is a supplied internal source, not independent proof of title.

**Push back:** require independent verification of ownership, encumbrances and authority, supported by appropriate external searches and underlying ownership/transfer and authority evidence. Maintain the separate fundamental/title warranty regime regardless of the register.

### 8. Lease and Mossvale: avoid inventing consent requirements
- **Office lease:** the supplied summary identifies notification, not landlord consent. Verify and arrange compliance with the actual notice obligation.
- **Mossvale:** an assignment restriction does not itself establish a consent requirement for a share sale. Review the complete agreement for any distinct change-control provision before requiring consent.

## Recommended negotiating priorities

1. **Reset the liability framework:** 25% cap, AUD 5,000 de minimis, AUD 50,000 tipping basket and 24 months; separate fundamental/title protection and mandatory misconduct carve-outs.
2. **Reject risk-shifting shortcuts:** blanket disclosure, buyer-knowledge exclusions and “all Claims” overrides; keep Tax/IP open.
3. **Secure Completion outcomes:** effective Bluefen consent with satisfied conditions; Riverlark payout and releases; explicit bonus funding; verified title and Ironquay cure.
4. **Refresh the evidence:** obtain the current underlying DD record, investigate the incident and assess renewals without unsupported conclusions.
5. **Record authority accurately:** no fallback is approved, no Seller label binds Buyer, and any permitted concession must pass our own approval process.

**MEMORANDUM**

**TO:** Wattlebridge Holdings Deal Team (Project Kestrel)  
**FROM:** Legal Counsel  
**DATE:** 24 September 2026  
**SUBJECT:** Project Kestrel — Review of Seller Draft SPA & Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

---

### EXECUTIVE SUMMARY & TACTICAL OVERVIEW

We have conducted a comprehensive review of the draft Share Purchase Agreement (SPA) positions, Disclosure Letter (SPA-003), and accompanying notes submitted by counsel for Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller). 

**Preliminary Warning on Seller Tactics:**  
The Seller’s draft contains aggressive procedural framing, including:
1. Labeling critical clauses as `[STANDARD]` and asserting they were "settled at principal level" or reflect "standard market terms."
2. Including an explicit instruction ("REVIEWER EFFICIENCY NOTE") directing us to ignore `[STANDARD]` provisions and focus only on `[OPEN]` items.

**We must reject these pre-categorisations entirely.** The Seller’s draft departs substantially from the Buyer Negotiation Playbook across nearly every key term. Furthermore, **no prior written authority has been granted by Amelia Frost** to accept any conditional fallbacks (such as a 20% cap or an 18-month warranty period). 

Below is our detailed critique of the Seller's draft against our Playbook, followed by actionable negotiation recommendations.

---

### DETAILED COMPARATIVE ANALYSIS & PLAYBOOK DEPARTURES

#### 1. Liability Package (Caps, Baskets, and Time Limits)
* **General Liability Cap (Clause 12.1):**
  * *Seller Draft:* Proposed at **20% of Purchase Price (AUD 4,800,000)**.
  * *Playbook Position:* Baseline is **25% / AUD 6,000,000**. The 20% cap is a conditional fallback requiring Amelia Frost’s explicit written approval specifying the draft. No such approval exists.
  * *Action:* Revert to **25% / AUD 6,000,000**.
* **De Minimis & Basket Thresholds (Clause 12.2):**
  * *Seller Draft:* De minimis of **AUD 25,000**; deductible basket of **AUD 250,000** (Seller liable for excess only).
  * *Playbook Position:* De minimis of **AUD 5,000**; aggregate basket of **AUD 50,000**, structured as a **tipping basket** (Seller liable from the *first dollar* once reached).
  * *Action:* Reject AUD 25k / AUD 250k deductible structure. Re-insert **AUD 5,000 de minimis** and **AUD 50,000 first-dollar tipping basket**.
* **General Claims Period (Clause 12.3 / 13):**
  * *Seller Draft:* **18 months** post-Completion.
  * *Playbook Position:* **24 months** post-Completion (18 months is a fallback requiring Amelia Frost’s approval, which has not been granted).
  * *Action:* Re-insert **24 months**.
* **Fundamental & Title Claims Regime:**
  * *Seller Draft:* Submits capacity and title warranties to the general regime (20% cap, 18-month limit, basket/de minimis).
  * *Playbook Position:* Must be a completely separate regime: **100% Purchase Price cap**, minimum **6-year limitation period**, and strictly carved out from general baskets, de minimis, and knowledge exclusions.
  * *Action:* Carve Title and Fundamental Warranties out into a standalone regime with 100% cap and 6-year term.
* **Fraud & Deliberate Misconduct Carve-Out (Clauses 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5):**
  * *Seller Draft:* Applies limitations, exclusive remedies, and non-reliance clauses universally to "all Claims of any nature."
  * *Playbook Position:* Fraud, wilful concealment, and deliberate misconduct must be expressly carved out from **all** caps, time limits, baskets, exclusive remedies, and non-reliance provisions.
  * *Action:* Insert explicit, non-negotiable fraud carve-outs across all limitation provisions.

---

#### 2. Disclosure Regime & Buyer Knowledge
* **General / Deemed Disclosure (Schedule 7 & Disclosure Letter 1.1–1.2):**
  * *Seller Draft:* Deems the entire data room (DD-002 to DD-012), statutory registers, and public registers broadly disclosed against all warranties.
  * *Playbook Position:* Reject blanket data-room or public-register disclosures. Require specific, fair disclosure with sufficient detail for the Buyer to evaluate the precise risk.
  * *Action:* Delete broad data-room/public search deemed disclosure clauses; insist on specific fair disclosure standard.
* **Buyer Knowledge Qualification (Clause 8.3):**
  * *Seller Draft:* Completely bars claims if the Buyer or its advisers had actual or constructive knowledge ("discoverable from the data room or public records").
  * *Playbook Position:* Delete blanket buyer-knowledge exclusions. Constructive knowledge ("discoverable") is unacceptable. Any knowledge qualification must be strictly limited to actual knowledge of named Seller key personnel after reasonable enquiry, and must **never** qualify Title, Capacity, Fraud, or Specific Indemnities.
  * *Action:* Delete Clause 8.3 constructive knowledge language and align seller knowledge qualifiers with named individuals and reasonable enquiry standards.

---

#### 3. Key Operational & Customer Conditions (Bluefen & Riverlark)
* **Bluefen Contract Consent (Clauses 3 / 6.3 & Disclosure Letter 2):**
  * *Seller Draft:* Seller offers "reasonable endeavours" and deems consent satisfied upon mere *delivery* of counterparty consent. Disclosure Letter 2 confirms no final consent or condition-satisfaction proof is currently provided.
  * *Playbook Position:* Bluefen represents ~30% FY26 revenue (~AUD 3.6m). Reasonable endeavours is insufficient. We require **effective consent AND verified evidence** that all associated conditions (clause 11.3) are satisfied **prior to Completion** (Condition Precedent), not post-delivery deeming.
  * *Action:* Make Bluefen consent and condition-satisfaction a strict Closing Condition Precedent.
* **Riverlark Debt & Security Release (Clauses 2 / 7 & Disclosure Letter 3):**
  * *Seller Draft:* Outstanding ~AUD 3.2m facility to be discharged post-Completion.
  * *Playbook Position:* Must be debt-free at Completion. We require a current payout figure, direct repayment from Completion funds, and effective security releases at Completion. A post-completion release is acceptable *only* with an irrevocable undertaking and Amelia Frost’s prior written approval (neither of which is present).
  * *Action:* Require direct debt payoff at closing via funds flow and delivery of executed release of security documents at Completion.

---

* **Employee Completion Bonuses (DD-005 & Disclosure Letter 5):**
  * *Seller Draft:* Excludes AUD 420,000 completion bonuses (and associated on-costs) from the draft Completion funds flow, claiming it is an internal Seller matter.
  * *Playbook Position:* Must be explicitly itemised in the Completion funds flow as a Seller-funded deduction from the purchase price, inclusive of all triggered

text:
# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller Update Draft and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

**Prepared for:** Wattlebridge Holdings deal team
**Basis:** Seller cover note and Disclosure Letter only. I have not seen the full SPA text or the underlying DD documents, so clause references follow the Seller's numbering and should be checked against the operative draft.

---

## 1. Headline view

The Seller calls this package "fair and balanced." It is not. Taken one at a time, the individual numbers (cap, basket, time limit) are within or near market range. **The real problem is how the provisions work together.** Four of them combine to remove almost all of our recourse for the problems we already know about:

1. **General disclosure** of the whole data room and public registers (DL 1.1–1.2).
2. **Buyer knowledge exclusion**, which covers both actual knowledge and anything "discoverable" (cl 8.3).
3. **Limitations apply to "all Claims of any nature"** (cl 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5, and the "unless expressly stated otherwise" default in 12.3/13).
4. **Title, capacity, tax and IP are folded into the general regime.**

Under this package, every known issue would be "disclosed" and "known." That covers Riverlark, Bluefen, Ironquay, the bonuses, the DD-006 incident and Sandbar. We would therefore have **no warranty claim** for any of them. Any residual claim would also be capped at AUD 4.8m, sit behind a AUD 250k deductible, and expire after 18 months.

The Disclosure Letter itself also contradicts the Seller's cover note on several points. **Read the cover note as advocacy, not as a statement of fact:**

| Item | Cover note says | Disclosure Letter says |
|---|---|---|
| Bluefen | "addressed" | no final consent, no evidence conditions satisfied (DL 2) |
| Riverlark | release "following Completion" | not repaid, no discharge (DL 3) |
| DD-006 | "not expected to be material" | access, scope and notification obligation not established (DL 6) |
| Sandbar | "ordinary-course" | Seller does *not* state they are ordinary course (DL 8) |
| Title | "evidenced" by register | register is only the source relied on; no verification (DL 10) |

---

## 2. Structural issues (the limitation architecture)

### 2.1 Limitations applying to "all Claims of any nature" (cl 9.3, 12.3/13, 12.8, 20.5)

**Seller position:** Caps, thresholds, time limits, exclusive remedy and non-reliance apply to every Claim unless expressly excluded.

**Why it matters:** As drafted, the wording would arguably cap or bar:
- specific indemnities, including the existing Ironquay indemnity;
- tax indemnity claims;
- leakage claims and completion-accounts or price-adjustment amounts;
- breach of pre-completion covenants and completion obligations;
- fraud, wilful misconduct and deliberate concealment.

The non-reliance and exclusive-remedy wording also aims to shut out claims for misleading or deceptive conduct under the Australian Consumer Law (s 18). Fraud cannot be fully contracted out of in any event, but we should not leave the point arguable.

**Push back:**
- Reverse the default. Limitations in cl 12 apply **only to general Warranty Claims**.
- Add express carve-outs from all limitations for:
  - fraud, dishonesty, wilful misconduct or concealment by the Seller or its representatives (including Company management acting before Completion);
  - Fundamental Warranties, the Tax Indemnity and specific indemnities (which get their own regime: see 2.2 and section 3);
  - leakage, price adjustment, covenant breaches and completion deliverables.
- Non-reliance must not exclude liability for the Warranties, the Disclosure Letter, or fraud.

### 2.2 Fundamental warranties (title and capacity) under the general cap and time limit

**Seller position:** The same cap and time limits as general warranties, "for administrative simplicity."

**Why it matters:** Title and capacity are the core of what we are paying for. If the shares are not validly owned, unencumbered and fully issued, the whole AUD 24m is at risk. A AUD 4.8m cap and an 18-month limit are not acceptable for title.

**Push back:**
- Cap at **100% of the purchase price**.
- Time limit of **at least 6 years** (aligned with the NSW limitation period for contract), with no de minimis or basket.
- Not qualified by disclosure or Buyer knowledge.

### 2.3 Title evidenced only by the share register (DD-012)

**Why it matters:** The Seller's own DL 10 concedes the register is simply "the source relied on." It is not verification. A register on its own does not exclude:
- unregistered issues or transfers;
- options, convertible notes, SAFEs or ESOP entitlements;
- shareholder agreement pre-emption rights;
- security over the shares (including any Riverlark security over Seller's shares);
- discrepancies with ASIC records.

**Push back:**
- Full title warranty package: legal and beneficial ownership, fully paid, no Encumbrances, no options or convertibles, no rights to call for issue of shares, and valid issue history.
- Our own reconciliation of the register against ASIC searches, PPSR searches (against both the Seller and the Company) and the constitution and shareholder agreement.
- Completion deliverables: executed transfers, share certificates or lost-certificate indemnities, any pre-emption waivers, and PPSR releases.

### 2.4 General disclosure (DL 1.1–1.2, Schedule 7)

**Seller position:** Everything in the data room as at 22 September 2026 (DD-002 to DD-012), plus the Accounts, statutory registers and public records, is disclosed against all warranties.

**Why it matters:** This converts our due diligence exercise into a waiver. We would also be bearing the risk of any document in the data room whose significance is not obvious on its face.

**Push back:**
- Delete general disclosure of the data room and "publicly searchable corporate records."
- At most, accept disclosure of the specific documents listed in the Disclosure Letter, and only to the extent **fairly disclosed**. That means with sufficient detail for a reasonable buyer to identify the nature, scope and *financial effect* of the matter.
- Disclosure qualifies Warranties only. It never qualifies Fundamental Warranties, the Tax Indemnity or specific indemnities.
- No updating or supplemental disclosure between signing and Completion may cure a breach. If one is offered, it should trigger only a Buyer termination right.
- Provide that DL 1.4 (non-admission) and DL 11 (reservation) do not dilute the specific disclosures. In particular, the Seller cannot rely on a disclosure as "fair" while also declining to say whether anything is required or material.

### 2.5 Buyer knowledge exclusion (cl 8.3)

**Seller position:** No claim for any matter the Buyer *or its advisers* knew of, "including any matter discoverable" from the data room or public records.

**Why it matters:**
- This is a constructive-knowledge exclusion and is broader than general disclosure.
- It imputes our advisers' knowledge to us.
- Read literally, it would defeat the specific indemnities we need for matters we already know about, which is exactly why those indemnities exist.

**Push back:** Delete cl 8.3. Replace it with an express provision that the Buyer's rights are not affected by any investigation or by any knowledge, actual, constructive or imputed, other than matters fairly disclosed in the Disclosure Letter. Our fallback position is *actual* knowledge of named individual deal team members only, and never applied to Fundamental Warranties, tax or indemnities.

### 2.6 Cap, de minimis and basket (cl 12.1–12.2)

| Term | Seller | Comment | Buyer ask |
|---|---|---|---|
| General cap | 20% (AUD 4.8m) | Within market for a non-W&I deal | Accept 20–30%, *provided* the carve-outs above are agreed. Otherwise hold out for higher. |
| De minimis | AUD 25k (~0.1%) | Broadly market | Accept, but aggregate claims arising from the same or related facts |
| Basket | AUD 250k (~1.04%), **excess only** (deductible) | The deductible structure is the main issue | **Tipping basket**: once exceeded, recover from dollar one. Threshold at 0.5–1% (AUD 120k–240k). |
| Time limit | 18 months | Market for general warranties | Accept 18–24 months for general. Tax 5–7 years (to cover ATO amendment periods plus a buffer). Fundamental 6+ years. |

**Consider warranty and indemnity (W&I) insurance.** If we take a W&I policy, a lower seller cap becomes more acceptable. However, known issues (all of section 3) will be excluded from W&I cover. That makes the specific indemnities and escrow below non-negotiable either way.

### 2.7 Tax and IP "settled under the general regime"

**Push back:**
- **Tax:** a standalone dollar-for-dollar tax indemnity for pre-Completion tax (including payroll tax, superannuation guarantee and PAYG on the DD-005 bonuses). It should be capped at 100% of price, last at least 5–7 years, and not be subject to the de minimis, basket or disclosure. Add conduct-of-claims provisions.
- **IP:** given the Ironquay chain-of-title gap, the IP warranties should at minimum sit outside the general basket. Ideally they should have an elevated cap (for example 50–100%) and a 3-year time limit.

---

## 3. Specific known issues

### 3.1 Bluefen: change-control consent (≈30% of FY26 revenue)

**Seller position:** Reasonable endeavours. The condition is treated as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

**Why it matters:**
- Bluefen accounts for about AUD 3.6m of revenue (around 30%), so it drives a material part of our valuation.
- DD-002 cl 11.3 attaches *conditions* to consent, and DL 2 confirms there is no evidence those conditions are satisfied.
- A bare "written consent" could be conditional, could carry adverse amendments (price, term, termination for convenience), or could leave the Company in default under 11.3.
- "Reasonable endeavours" is a weak obligation.

**Push back:**
- **Condition precedent:** an unconditional written consent from Bluefen (or a consent on terms satisfactory to the Buyer acting reasonably), with all cl 11.3 conditions satisfied or waived by Bluefen. No amendment to the Bluefen contract without Buyer consent.
- **Buyer-only waiver.** The Seller cannot deem the condition satisfied.
- Upgrade to **all reasonable endeavours**, with Buyer participation in engagement with Bluefen.
- Long-stop date with a Buyer walk-away right.
- Consider protection for the period after Completion, such as an escrow or price adjustment if Bluefen terminates or materially reduces volumes within an agreed period (for example 12 months) for a reason linked to the change of control.

### 3.2 Riverlark facility (≈AUD 3.2m outstanding)

**Seller position:** Release "to be provided following Completion."

**Why it matters:**
- This is inconsistent with the debt-free/cash-free basis.
- The change-of-control clause (DD-003 cl 8.1) is likely to trigger at Completion. It could cause a default or acceleration, and possibly cross-defaults, against a company we now own.
- Until discharge under cl 9.2, the Company's assets, and possibly the shares, stay encumbered.
- A promise to deliver a release after Completion leaves us chasing the Seller once we have already paid.

**Push back:**
- Repay at Completion out of the purchase price, as a line item in the funds flow paid directly to Riverlark.
- **Completion deliverables:** a payoff letter confirming the exact payoff amount (including break costs and accrued interest); an executed deed of release; PPSR financing change statements (or an undertaking to lodge them within 1–2 business days, backed by an irrevocable authority); and return of any title documents.
- The full payoff amount is treated as Debt in the price mechanics.
- Seller indemnity for any residual Riverlark liability.

### 3.3 DD-005 completion bonuses (AUD 420,000)

**Seller position:** "A matter for the Seller"; not itemised in the funds flow.

**Why it matters:** These are almost certainly the *Company's* obligations as employer, not the Seller's. Unless they are dealt with in the funds flow, we inherit them at full value, together with on-costs. DL 5 expressly declines to say whether payroll tax, superannuation and other on-costs apply. Our estimate is that the true cost is materially above AUD 420k once those are included. The "continued employment" conditions also need clarifying. If any portion vests after Completion, the cost could fall on us post-Completion.

**Push back:**
- Treat the bonuses plus all associated on-costs (employer superannuation, payroll tax, workers' compensation, and any PAYG withholding mechanics) as **Transaction Expenses / Debt-like items** deducted from the price.
- Pay them through Company payroll at or immediately after Completion, funded from the Seller's proceeds.
- Specific indemnity outside the limitations.
- Obtain the bonus letters and confirm the exact vesting conditions and any amounts payable after Completion. Any retention we want to keep should be negotiated as *our* arrangement, not inherited.

### 3.4 Ironquay: SOW3 IP and the AUD 180,000 open payment

**Seller position:** The existing indemnity covers only the specific SOW3 payment, which the Seller says is adequate.

**Why it matters:** The real risk is **IP ownership**, not the AUD 180k. Under DD-004 cl 7.3, title to the SOW3 Project Materials only passes on cleared payment of *every* SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180k open, and no receipt or confirmatory assignment exists. The Company may therefore not own IP that may be integral to its product. That exposes us to:
- infringement claims;
- injunctions;
- re-development costs;
- customer warranty breaches;
- leverage for Ironquay in negotiations.

An indemnity limited to the fee does not address any of these.

**Push back:**
- **CP or Completion deliverable:** evidence of cleared payment of all SOW3 fees, plus an executed **confirmatory IP assignment deed** from Ironquay covering all SOW3 Project Materials, with moral rights consents where relevant.
- If this cannot be obtained before Completion, an **expanded specific indemnity** covering all Loss arising from any defect in the Company's title to, or right to use, Ironquay deliverables. That includes third-party claims, re-development and remediation costs, and customer claims. It should sit outside the cap, basket, time limit, disclosure and knowledge exclusions, and be backed by escrow.
- Confirm whether SOW1, SOW2 or any later SOWs carry the same retention-of-title mechanism.

### 3.5 DD-006 export / privacy incident (~1,240 records)

**Seller position:** A "preliminary operational matter," not expected to be material.

**Why it matters:**
- A download link sent to an unintended external address, involving names, business emails, roles and activity timestamps, is a potential eligible data breach under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) Notifiable Data Breaches scheme.
- Where an entity suspects an eligible data breach, it must carry out an assessment and is generally expected to complete it within 30 days. The incident was known by at least 22 September 2026. Depending on when the Company first became aware, that window **may already have passed**. A failure to assess or notify is itself a compliance exposure.
- Penalty exposure under the Privacy Act regime is significant. There may also be contractual notification obligations to customers, potentially including Bluefen, which interacts with 3.1.
- DL 6 confirms nothing has been established: not access, not scope, and not whether notification is required.

**Push back:**
- **Immediate information request:** incident timeline (date of awareness), the investigation or forensic report, access logs for the link, whether the link has been revoked, the notification analysis, any OAIC or customer correspondence, and customer contract notification clauses.
- **Pre-Completion covenant:** the Company completes the assessment promptly with Buyer input and makes any required notifications. No admissions or regulator engagement without Buyer consultation.
- **Specific indemnity:** regulatory penalties (to the extent lawfully indemnifiable), investigation and notification costs, third-party and customer claims, and remediation. It should sit outside all limitations and be backed by escrow.
- Warranty that there are no other privacy or security incidents.

### 3.6 Sandbar supplier renewals (3 × AUD 110,000 = AUD 330,000)

**Seller position:** Ordinary-course operating costs.

**Why it matters:** DL 8 asks us to read DD-008 and DD-011 "together for timing/scope," and the Seller *declines* to state they are ordinary course. We see three identical renewals that are "related." That pattern is consistent with a single commitment being split to fall below an approval or conduct-of-business threshold. If the renewals were entered into close to signing or Completion, or with a related party, they may also be leakage.

**Push back:**
- Information request on the dates, term, termination rights, prepayment or accrual position, whether Sandbar is a related party, and internal approvals.
- Aggregate related transactions in the conduct-of-business covenants so they cannot be split below thresholds.
- If any renewal is not genuinely needed or not ordinary course, require termination at the Seller's cost before Completion, or a price adjustment or specific indemnity.
- If Sandbar is a Seller affiliate, treat payments as Leakage.
- Ensure any accrued or prepaid amounts are correctly reflected in completion accounts or net debt.

### 3.7 Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009): lower risk, but verify

The Seller's characterisation is plausible: the lease requires notification rather than consent, and the Mossvale restriction covers assignment rather than change of control. We should still **check this ourselves rather than rely on DL 1.4/11 wording.** In particular, check whether "assignment" in DD-009 is defined to include change of control.

- Make the lease notification a Completion deliverable or post-Completion covenant.
- Obtain a warranty that no material contract contains a change-of-control right other than Bluefen and Riverlark.

---

## 4. Indicative known-issue exposure

| Item | Indicative amount | Recovery under Seller's package |
|---|---|---|
| Riverlark facility | ~AUD 3.2m | Nil if treated as disclosed or known |
| DD-005 bonuses + on-costs | AUD 420k + on-costs | Nil ("matter for Seller" but sits in Company) |
| Sandbar renewals | AUD 330k | Nil |
| Ironquay fee + IP title | AUD 180k + unquantified IP risk | Fee-only indemnity, possibly capped |
| DD-006 incident | Unquantified (regulatory, notification, claims) | Nil |
| Bluefen | ~AUD 3.6m annual revenue at risk | No protection beyond a weak CP |

Quantifiable items alone come to **roughly AUD 4.1m or more**, before Bluefen, IP and privacy exposures. That is about 17% of the price.

---

## 5. Summary of recommendations

**Priority 1: deal-critical (reject outright)**
1. **Limit the limitations.** Caps, thresholds, time limits, exclusive remedy and non-reliance apply to general Warranty Claims only. Carve out fraud, wilful concealment, Fundamental Warranties, tax, specific indemnities, leakage and covenant or completion obligations.
2. **Fundamental warranties:** cap at 100% of price, 6+ years, no thresholds, not qualified by disclosure or knowledge. Verify title independently (ASIC and PPSR searches, constitution and shareholder agreement, no options or convertibles). The register alone is not enough.
3. **Delete general disclosure** (data room and public records). Only specific, fair disclosure; no cure by updated disclosure.
4. **Delete the Buyer knowledge exclusion** (cl 8.3). Replace with an express statement that the Buyer's rights are not affected by investigation or knowledge.
5. **Riverlark:** repay at Completion from proceeds, with payoff letter, deed of release and PPSR discharges as Completion deliverables. Treat as Debt.
6. **Bluefen:** unconditional consent with cl 11.3 conditions satisfied as a Buyer-only waivable CP, all reasonable endeavours, long-stop walk-away, and consider post-Completion revenue protection.

**Priority 2: specific indemnities, price and escrow**

7. **DD-005 bonuses:** deduct the bonuses plus all on-costs from the price as Transaction Expenses, paid through payroll. Add an indemnity.
8. **Ironquay:** payment and confirmatory IP assignment as a Completion deliverable. Otherwise, a broad IP title indemnity outside the limitations.
9. **DD-006:** urgent information request, a pre-Completion assessment and notification covenant, and a broad specific indemnity.
10. **Escrow or retention:** negotiate an escrow (indicatively AUD 1.5–2.5m, about 6–10% of price, for 12–24 months) to secure the Ironquay, DD-006 and Bluefen-related protections.
11. **Sandbar:** diligence the related renewals, aggregate thresholds in the conduct covenants, and treat as Leakage or adjust price if not ordinary course or if a related party.
12. **Standalone tax indemnity:** 100% cap, 5–7 years, covering payroll tax and super on the bonuses.

**Priority 3: commercial terms (negotiable)**

13. Cap of 20–30% for general warranties is acceptable *if* items 1–4 are won.
14. **Tipping basket** at 0.5–1%. De minimis of AUD 25k is acceptable, with aggregation of related claims.
15. General warranty period of 18–24 months is acceptable. IP warranties should have an elevated cap and a longer period.
16. Lease and Mossvale: verify independently. Add a no-other-change-of-control warranty.
17. Consider **W&I insurance** for unknown risks. Note it will not cover the known issues above, so items 5–12 must be dealt with in the SPA regardless.

**Immediate information requests to the Seller:**
- Bluefen consent correspondence and cl 11.3 status;
- Riverlark payoff figure and break costs;
- bonus letters and on-cost calculation;
- Ironquay payment status, all SOWs, and willingness to sign a confirmatory assignment;
- DD-006 timeline, investigation report, link access logs and notification analysis;
- Sandbar contracts, dates, approvals and related-party status;
- full capitalisation table, plus confirmation of no options, convertibles or share security.

*Clause references should be checked against the operative SPA draft before the mark-up is issued. Privacy, tax and employment points should be confirmed with specialist advisers.*

# Project Kestrel — Buyer-Side Review of Seller's SPA Positions & Disclosure Letter

Before the substance, one procedural flag that colours everything below.

## 0. Ignore the "Reviewer Efficiency Note" — it is a negotiating device, not a fact

The Seller's note asserts that clauses marked **[STANDARD]** have "been reviewed and cleared by both sides and need no further scrutiny." **That is not true, and we have not agreed any of it.** Almost every item they have labelled [STANDARD] is in fact a materially seller-favourable position that cuts directly against your interests. Treating the label as settled is exactly how a buyer gives away its most important protections. We review everything on the merits. I'd also push back on this framing in writing so it isn't later characterised as accepted by conduct.

---

## Material issues, with reasoning

### 1. Fundamental/Title warranties capped like general warranties (serious)
The Seller wants capacity and title warranties "subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity." This is the single biggest giveaway. Title and capacity go to whether you actually get what you are paying AUD 24m for. Market standard is that these are capped at **100% of price** and survive for **6–7 years** (often statutory limitation). Accepting a 20% cap (AUD 4.8m) and an 18-month survival means that if title fails, you could lose the company and recover only a fraction. **Reject outright.** Push for 100% cap, 6+ year survival.

### 2. 20% general cap / de minimis / basket (negotiable but not "standard")
- **Cap at 20% (AUD 4.8m):** within market range (often 10–30%) but should be negotiated knowingly, and *tax and fundamental warranties must sit outside it*.
- **Basket AUD 250,000 "excess only" (deductible/tipping):** the Seller has chosen a pure deductible (recover only excess). Push for a *threshold/tipping basket* (once exceeded, recover from first dollar), or at least negotiate the number down relative to a AUD 24m deal.
- **De minimis AUD 25,000:** acceptable in principle; confirm aggregation rules for related claims.

### 3. "All limitations apply to all Claims unless expressly stated" — carve-outs needed (serious)
Clauses 9.3 / 12.3 / 12.8 / 13 / 20.5 push every limitation, time bar, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provision across **all** claims. Standard buyer carve-outs must survive: **fraud, wilful concealment, fundamental/title warranties, tax, and the specific indemnities** (Ironquay, and any new indemnities below). As drafted, fraud could be swept under an 18-month bar and a 20% cap — unacceptable.

### 4. Buyer knowledge / anti-sandbagging + general disclosure (serious — combine with Disclosure Letter)
Clause 8.3 bars any claim for matters the Buyer "or its advisers had knowledge" of, **including anything discoverable from the data room or public records.** Read with Disclosure Letter [1.1]–[1.2], which "discloses every fact … contained or referred to in" the entire data room (DD-002–DD-012) plus all public registers.

Combined effect: the Seller deems the **entire data room generally disclosed** *and* bars you from claiming on anything "discoverable" there. This guts the warranties — the known problem items (below) would all be disclosed away. Push back hard:
- Delete the "discoverable" / constructive-knowledge language; limit to the *actual knowledge* of named deal individuals.
- Require **specific, fair disclosure** with sufficient detail to identify the matter and its impact — reject sweeping "deemed disclosure of everything in the data room."
- Note [1.4] says nothing admits liability/materiality/that any consent is required — standard reservation, but it means disclosure is being used to shift risk without conceding anything.

### 5. Bluefen consent — a real closing risk dressed as [STANDARD] (serious)
Bluefen is **~30% of revenue (~AUD 3.6m)** with a change-of-control consent (cl. 11.2/11.3 conditions). The Disclosure Letter admits **no final written consent and no evidence conditions are satisfied.** The Seller wants this to be a mere "reasonable endeavours" condition, "treated as satisfied on delivery of … written consent."
- Make the actual, unconditional Bluefen consent (with 11.3 conditions satisfied) a **hard condition precedent to Completion**, not a reasonable-endeavours best-efforts item.
- Given revenue concentration, consider a **specific indemnity / price adjustment / earn-out protection** if Bluefen terminates post-Completion.

### 6. Riverlark facility — "release following Completion" is backwards (serious)
~AUD 3.2m facility with change-of-control (8.1) and security/discharge (9.2); **not repaid, no discharge in the data room.** Seller proposes release *after* Completion. In a **debt-free/cash-free** deal you must not take the company still encumbered.
- Require **repayment and discharge of security at or before Completion** (deducted from proceeds via funds flow), with a **payout letter and deed of release/release of PPSR charges** as a condition/completion deliverable. Do not accept a post-Completion promise.

### 7. Ironquay IP — indemnity too narrow, and an IP-ownership risk (serious)
DD-004 cl. 7.3: transfer of **SOW3 Project Materials is conditional on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee**; DD-010 shows **AUD 180,000 open**, with no proof of payment and **no confirmatory assignment** in the data room. So the Company may **not own key IP** until paid. Seller limits the indemnity to "the specific SOW3 payment."
- The exposure is not just the AUD 180k — it's **loss/encumbrance of the IP itself**. Require (a) evidence SOW3 is paid and a signed assignment delivered pre-Completion, or (b) a **broad indemnity covering IP ownership/title failure and consequential loss**, uncapped by the general cap.
- Confirm no other SOW fees outstanding.

### 8. DD-005 closing bonuses AUD 420,000 — must hit the funds flow (moderate)
Conditional Completion bonuses of AUD 420k are triggered **by Completion** but are **omitted from the funds flow**, and the Seller says they're "a matter for the Seller." In a debt-free/cash-free deal, a liability *triggered by the transaction* is economically the Seller's.
- Treat as a **Completion/transaction cost borne by Seller** — deduct from proceeds or include as a defined Leakage/Seller liability.
- Also capture **payroll tax, superannuation and on-costs** (disclosure is silent) — the true number exceeds AUD 420k.

### 9. DD-006 export/privacy incident — not "immaterial" (serious)
~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps) sent to an unintended external address. Seller calls it "preliminary… not expected to be material." The disclosure admits scope/access/notification obligations are **unresolved**. This is a potential **Privacy Act / Notifiable Data Breach** matter with regulatory, notification and remediation exposure.
- Require a **specific indemnity** for all losses, regulatory penalties, notification and remediation costs arising from DD-006, uncapped and surviving beyond 18 months.
- Add a condition for the Seller to complete the investigation / provide a status report pre-Completion.

### 10. Lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009) consents (moderate)
Seller characterises these as not requiring consent for a *share* sale. Possibly correct (share sale ≠ assignment), but **verify the actual clauses** — some leases/contracts define change of control as a trigger. At minimum obtain a bring-down warranty that no counterparty consent is required or, if any is, that it's obtained. Confirm the DD-007 **notification obligation** is complied with to avoid default.

### 11. Sandbar supplier renewals AUD 330,000 (minor–moderate)
Three related renewals; disclosure won't say whether avoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course. Seller calls them "ordinary-course operating costs." Diligence whether these are **committed liabilities** that should be reflected in the debt-free/cash-free/net-working-capital mechanics rather than absorbed by you.

### 12. Tax and IP warranties "settled under the general regime" (serious)
Tax should **never** sit under an 18-month / 20% general regime — it must have its own **longer survival (to statutory limitation, typically 7 years)** and ideally a **separate tax deed/indemnity**. IP warranties (ownership, non-infringement, no encumbrance) matter enormously for an analytics business and should be full, with the Ironquay issue specifically addressed. Reject the "settled" characterisation.

### 13. Title evidenced only by share register (DD-012) (moderate)
Title "evidenced by the Company share register" is a starting point, not full comfort. Require: full warranty of unencumbered title, **no PPSR/other security over the shares**, Harbourglass's capacity/authority, and standard Completion deliverables (share transfers, resignations, registers, consents). This links to issue 1 — title warranty must carry a 100% cap.

---

## Summary of recommendations (priority order)

**Reject / hard-line:**
1. **Fundamental & title warranties:** 100% cap, 6–7 yr survival — not the general 20%/18-month regime.
2. **Tax:** separate indemnity/deed, survival to statutory limitation, outside general cap.
3. **Carve-outs** from all caps/time bars/exclusive-remedy/non-reliance for **fraud, title, tax, and specific indemnities**.
4. **Riverlark:** repay + discharge security *at/before* Completion via funds flow; payout letter + release as conditions. No post-Completion promise.
5. **Bluefen:** actual unconditional consent as a **condition precedent**; revenue-concentration protection.
6. **Anti-sandbagging / deemed data-room disclosure:** delete "discoverable"/constructive-knowledge wording; require **specific, fair** disclosure only.

**Secure specific indemnities (uncapped by general cap, longer survival):**
7. **DD-006 privacy/export incident** — full regulatory/notification/remediation cover.
8. **Ironquay/SOW3 IP** — IP ownership/title failure, not just the AUD 180k; deliver assignment + proof of payment.

**Economic/funds-flow adjustments:**
9. **DD-005 bonuses (AUD 420k + on-costs)** — Seller-borne, into funds flow/Leakage.
10. **Sandbar renewals (AUD 330k)** — reflect committed liabilities in the price mechanics.

**Diligence/verification before signing:**
11. Lease (DD-007) notification + consent, Mossvale (DD-009), and full title/PPSR verification — don't rely on the share register alone.

**Negotiate (knowingly, not as "standard"):**
12. General cap level; convert the basket to a **tipping/threshold** basket; confirm aggregation and de minimis mechanics.

**Procedural:**
13. **Reject the "[STANDARD] = cleared, no scrutiny" framing in writing.** Nothing has been agreed; we are marking up the full package.

---
*One caveat: this review is based on the Seller's summaries and Disclosure Letter, not the underlying SPA clause text or the DD-002–DD-012 documents themselves. Several conclusions (e.g. consent triggers, PPSR position, exact indemnity scope) need to be confirmed against the actual drafting and data-room contents. Happy to turn this into a mark-up/issues list for the SPA once we have the clause text.*

# Project Kestrel – Buyer Review of Seller Update & Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

**Preliminary note on the Seller's framing.** The "Preamble", "FINAL" labels, "[STANDARD] – cleared by both sides" tags and the "Reviewer Efficiency Note" are the Seller's assertions, not instructions to us. Nothing in our playbook records principal-level agreement on any of these points, and no written authority from Amelia Frost exists for any fallback. I have reviewed every clause in full, ignoring the pre-categorisation. The Seller's own Disclosure Letter (para 11) in fact confirms "no expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included" – which contradicts the covering note's claim that terms were settled.

---

**SPA-N-001: General liability cap**
- Seller: 20% / AUD 4,800,000.
- Buyer wants: 25% / AUD 6,000,000.
- Recommendation: **Reject; counter at 25% / AUD 6,000,000.** 20% is our conditional fallback only, usable solely with Amelia Frost's prior written authority identifying the draft – none has been given.

**SPA-N-002: De minimis & basket**
- Seller: de minimis AUD 25,000; basket AUD 250,000; excess-only recovery.
- Buyer wants: de minimis AUD 5,000; basket AUD 50,000; first-dollar recovery once exceeded.
- Recommendation: **Reject on all three elements.** Seller's thresholds are 5x ours and the "excess only" structure would forfeit the first AUD 250,000 of every claim set; first-dollar ("tipping") recovery is required.

**SPA-N-003: General claims time limit**
- Seller: 18 months, plus a drafting rule that any limitation applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.
- Buyer wants: 24 months; 18 months only with Amelia Frost written approval (none given).
- Recommendation: **Reject; counter at 24 months and delete the "applies to all Claims" default.** The default rule is a hidden override that would drag Fundamental/Title, Tax, IP and indemnity claims into the general period.

**SPA-N-004: Fundamental/Title regime**
- Seller: capacity and title warranties subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties "for administrative simplicity".
- Buyer wants: separate regime – 100% of price cap, at least six years, outside the general basket, de minimis and knowledge bar.
- Recommendation: **Reject outright.** Capping title at 20% would mean we could pay AUD 24m and recover at most AUD 4.8m if we did not get the shares; administrative simplicity is not a reason.

**SPA-N-005: Fraud carve-out**
- Seller: Clauses 9.3/12.8/20.5 apply limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance "to all Claims of any nature" – no fraud carve-out anywhere in the package.
- Buyer wants: fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct carved out of all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedies and non-reliance, to the maximum extent enforceable; non-waivable.
- Recommendation: **Insert an express carve-out; non-negotiable.** A limitation package with no fraud carve-out is unacceptable on principle and partially unenforceable in any event, so the Seller loses nothing legitimate by conceding it.

**SPA-N-006: Disclosure scope**
- Seller: general disclosure of the entire data room (DD-002 to DD-012), Accounts, statutory registers and publicly searchable records (Disclosure Letter 1.1–1.2; Schedule 7).
- Buyer wants: specific, fair disclosure only; no whole-data-room, public-register or prudent-search deemed disclosure.
- Recommendation: **Reject paras 1.1–1.2 and replace with a "fairly disclosed with sufficient detail to identify the nature and scope" standard, limited to the specific disclosures in section 2 onward.** Blanket data-room disclosure would effectively neutralise the warranties and compound the buyer-knowledge exclusion.

**SPA-N-007: Buyer knowledge qualifier**
- Seller: Clause 8.3 – no claim for any matter of which Buyer or advisers had knowledge, including anything "discoverable" from the data room or public records.
- Buyer wants: delete the blanket exclusion; any residual qualifier limited to actual knowledge of named Buyer individuals, with Seller warranty knowledge tied to named Seller persons after reasonable enquiry; never applies to title, capacity, fraud or specific indemnities.
- Recommendation: **Delete 8.3 in its entirety.** "Discoverable" is a constructive-knowledge test that shifts the Seller's disclosure burden onto us and overlaps with SPA-N-006 to gut the warranty package.

**SPA-N-008: Bluefen consent**
- Seller: reasonable endeavours only; consent deemed satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent. Disclosure Letter para 2 confirms no final consent and no evidence the clause 11.3 conditions are met.
- Buyer wants: effective (unconditional or conditions-satisfied) Bluefen consent as a condition precedent, with evidence of satisfaction of the 11.3 conditions delivered before Completion.
- Recommendation: **Reject consent-on-delivery and reasonable endeavours; require an all-reasonable/best-endeavours covenant plus a CP of effective consent with documentary evidence of 11.3 satisfaction.** Bluefen is ~30% of FY26 revenue (~AUD 3.6m); a conditional consent whose conditions are unmet is no protection at all.

**SPA-N-009: Riverlark facility**
- Seller: ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding; release "to be provided following Completion". Disclosure Letter para 3 confirms not repaid and no discharge in the data room.
- Buyer wants: current payout letter, direct repayment from Completion funds via the funds flow, and effective security releases (including PPSR discharge) delivered at Completion.
- Recommendation: **Reject post-completion release; require payout + direct repayment + releases as Completion deliverables.** We would otherwise acquire a company still encumbered by a ~AUD 3.2m secured facility in breach of its change-of-control clause 8.1; a post-completion release is only tolerable with an irrevocable bank undertaking and Amelia Frost approval, neither of which exists.

**SPA-N-010: Employee bonuses**
- Seller: DD-005 Completion bonuses of AUD 420,000 "a matter for the Seller" and not itemised in funds flow; Disclosure Letter para 5 confirms omission and is silent on payroll tax, super and on-costs.
- Buyer wants: AUD 420,000 plus triggered on-costs (superannuation, payroll tax, leave accruals) as a specific funds-flow line item or treated as Seller-funded/Debt-like, with a supporting on-cost schedule.
- Recommendation: **Reject the silent exclusion; require an itemised line and on-cost quantification.** Bonuses triggered by Completion are a Seller-caused liability landing in the Company we are buying debt-free/cash-free, and "a matter for the Seller" has no binding mechanism behind it.

**SPA-N-011: Ironquay IP indemnity**
- Seller: indemnity limited to the specific SOW3 payment; "considered adequate". Disclosure para 4 confirms DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open (not bank-verified), no receipt and no confirmatory assignment in the data room.
- Buyer wants: a broader indemnity covering any defect in title to or use of SOW3 Project Materials and consequential loss, while preserving the SOW3 payment cure; verification of the AUD 180,000 status either way; confirmatory assignment as a deliverable.
- Recommendation: **Broaden the indemnity and add a pre-Completion verification/cure step.** Under DD-004 cl 7.3 the Project Materials do not transfer until every SOW3 fee clears, so the IP risk is ownership, not just a AUD 180,000 payable – and we have not verified whether that sum is actually unpaid.

**SPA-N-012: Export/privacy incident**
- Seller: "preliminary operational matter", "not expected to be material". Disclosure para 6: link sent to an unintended external address; ~1,240 records; access, scope and notification duty all undetermined.
- Buyer wants: log preservation, a documented investigation, updates through to Completion, and a specific indemnity for notification/regulatory/remediation costs if a breach is confirmed; no assumption of breach or harm either way.
- Recommendation: **Reject the materiality characterisation; impose preservation/investigation/update covenants and a contingent specific indemnity.** No breach, harm or notification duty is established, but equally the Seller cannot assert immateriality on an incomplete investigation – and this item must not be caught by the general disclosure or knowledge bar.

**SPA-N-013: Sandbar renewals**
- Seller: AUD 330,000 (3 x AUD 110,000) are ordinary-course operating costs. Disclosure para 8: DD-008/DD-011 to be read together; silent on whether unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course.
- Buyer wants: a factual assessment (timing, termination rights, accrual status, whether triggered by Completion) before taking any position; no automatic Debt classification or price deduction.
- Recommendation: **Neither accept nor reject yet; request the DD-008/DD-011 contracts and accrual treatment and reserve the position.** The Seller's "ordinary course" label is unsupported by its own disclosure, but our playbook does not pre-judge a price adjustment.

**SPA-N-014: Category separation**
- Seller: single general regime for everything – "any limitation applies to all Claims unless expressly stated" (12.3), limitations/exclusive-remedy/non-reliance "to all Claims of any nature" (9.3/12.8/20.5), Tax and IP "settled under the general regime", Title folded into general.
- Buyer wants: Title/Fundamental, Tax, IP, payment/leakage and covenant/indemnity claims each with their own cap, period and threshold treatment, and an express clause that the general regime does not apply to them.
- Recommendation: **Reject; insert an express carve-out clause listing the separate categories.** The Seller's drafting works as a hidden override that collapses every negotiated protection back to 20% / 18 months / AUD 250k basket.

**SPA-N-015: Title verification**
- Seller: title evidenced by the share register at DD-012. Disclosure para 10 concedes this is merely the source relied on and that Buyer verification is not complete.
- Buyer wants: independent evidence – ASIC extract, PPSR search, Riverlark and any other encumbrance confirmations, Seller board/shareholder authority documents, and a warranty that the register is accurate and complete.
- Recommendation: **Do not accept DD-012 as proof; require the independent package as CPs/Completion deliverables.** The register is a Seller-supplied internal document and the Seller itself declines to say it has been verified.

**SPA-N-016: Tax/IP open terms**
- Seller: Tax and IP "settled under the general regime".
- Buyer wants: Tax and IP remain OPEN – separate warranties, a tax indemnity and (likely) longer periods/higher caps to be negotiated; no assumption of unlimited liability and no assumption these are resolved.
- Recommendation: **Reject "settled"; mark as OPEN in our mark-up and reserve all positions.** There has been no negotiation on these terms, and folding them into a 20%/18-month regime would be a concession made by default.

---

**Summary for the deal team**

| Status | Issues |
|---|---|
| Reject / counter with playbook position | 001, 002, 003, 004, 005, 006, 007, 008, 009, 010, 011, 014, 015 |
| Reject characterisation; impose covenants | 012 |
| Assess further; reserve | 013 |
| Mark OPEN | 016 |

Nothing in the Seller package meets a playbook position, and no fallback authority from Amelia Frost exists for any item. I'd suggest the covering response to Seller counsel state plainly that no terms are agreed at principal level, that the [STANDARD]/FINAL labelling is not accepted, and that the limitation package, disclosure framework and condition/deliverable mechanics are all re-opened. I can prepare the clause-by-clause mark-up next if useful.
